title: Build an agent that can use a tool
description: Connect a tool, return its results, and stop an agent when its task is done.
objective: Build a bounded loop that executes tool requests, returns matching results, and finishes with an answer supported by those results.

sources.claim: An agent can use tool feedback in a loop, with stopping conditions such as an iteration limit.
For client tools, the application executes a requested tool and returns a result associated with that request.

beats.title: Give the agent a way to check
beats.body: A user asks whether two items are in stock. The answer lives in an inventory, outside the model. You will build the loop around the model so it can request a lookup, receive the result, and answer. A tool call is a structured request to run a function. Our lookup_stock tool reads a local practice inventory. Model responses are simulated; the tool and the program you build execute in your browser. Use Step to follow one operation at a time, or Run to follow the whole loop.

beats.title: A request needs an executor
beats.goal: The model can request lookup_stock, but this program stops before executing the request. Predict its outcome, then run it. Inspect the request and the conversation.

beats.title: Connect the tool
beats.goal: Change the block that handles a tool request so it executes the lookup. Keep the other blocks fixed for this experiment. Predict what happens when the program runs the tool but discards its result.

beats.title: Make the result available
beats.goal: The tool ran, but the conversation did not receive its result. The conversation is the message history sent on the next model call. Change how the program handles the result. A call ID links each result to the request it answers. Run your repair and inspect both lookups.

beats.title: An answer and a limit are different exits
beats.body: Your program now runs both lookups and sends their results back. The next model response can contain a final answer. Return that answer and stop. Calling the model again after an answer wastes calls. Keep a maximum call count as a separate limit for unfinished work. Reaching that limit means the loop stopped; it does not mean the task succeeded. Next, repair both the result handling and the final-answer branch in a new program.

beats.title: Build a loop that works on fresh cases
beats.goal: Repair this program so it checks every requested item, returns the stock counts from the tool results, and stops before its call limit. Run tests the same program on three inventories. Inspect each case. The goal is a reusable loop, so changing an answer for one inventory cannot solve the task.

beats.title: You built the control loop
beats.body: Your program connected a model response to a tool, returned the observation with its call ID, and stopped when an answer arrived. The execution trace shows what happened at each step. Fresh inventories checked whether the same program could use different observations. This exercise uses a declared model simulation. A real model may choose different tools or produce invalid requests, so its behavior needs separate testing. Completing this practice is evidence about these loop mechanics, not a claim of general agent reliability.

beats.intro: Choose another inventory and change the loop. Try discarding a result, using an unrelated call ID, or continuing after an answer. Compare the trace and conversation. Free play does not change your challenge result.
